'''Tony Hilton Royle Skyrme''' ({{IPAc-en|s|k|ɜr|m}}; 5 December 1922 – 25 June 1987) was a [[British people|British]] [[physicist]] who was born in [[Lewisham]].

He proposed modelling the [[Mean field theory|effective interaction]] between [[nucleon]]s in [[Atomic nucleus|nuclei]] by a zero-range [[Scalar potential|potential]].<ref>{{Cite journal| first1 = T. . | title = The effective nuclear potential | journal = Nuclear Physics| last1 = Skyrme | volume = 9| issue = 4 | pages = 615–634 | year = 1959 | doi = 10.1016/0029-5582(58)90345-6|bibcode = 1958NucPh...9..615S }}</ref> This idea is still widely used today in [[nuclear structure]],<ref>{{Cite journal| first1 = M. .| first2 = P. H. | title = Self-consistent mean-field models for nuclear structure| last1 = Bender | journal = Reviews of Modern Physics | volume = 75 | issue = 1 | pages = 121–180 | year = 2003 | doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121| last2 = Heenen| bibcode=2003RvMP...75..121B}}</ref> and in [[equations of state]] for [[neutron star]]s.<ref name=Haensel>{{cite book |title=Neutron Stars |author1=Haensel, P. |author2=Potekhin, A. Y. |author3=Yakovlev, D. G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iIrj9nfHnesC |isbn=978-0-387-33543-8 |publisher=Springer |year=2007}}</ref>

Skyrme is perhaps best known for formulating the first [[topological soliton]] to model a particle, the [[skyrmion]].<ref>{{Cite journal| first1 = T. . | title = A unified field theory of mesons and baryons | journal = Nuclear Physics| last1 = Skyrme | volume = 31 | pages = 556–569 | year = 1962 | doi = 10.1016/0029-5582(62)90775-7|bibcode = 1962NucPh..31..556S }}</ref> Some of his most important work can be found in his selected papers.<ref name="Sel papers">{{cite book|last1=Skyrme and [[Gerald E. Brown]]|title=Selected Papers, with Commentary, of Tony Hilton Royle Skyrme|date=1994|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=9789812795922|pages=vi|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9gDwymeh0WIC|accessdate=1 February 2016}}</ref><ref>Brown G.E. (ed 1994) ''Selected papers, with commentary, of Tony Hilton Royle Skyrme''. World Scientific Series in 20th Century Physics: Volume 3. {{ISBN|978-981-4502-43-6}}</ref> Skyrme was awarded the [[Hughes Medal]] by the [[Royal Society]] in 1985.

==Life==
Tony Skyrme was born in [[Lewisham]], [[London]], the child of a bank clerk. He attended a boarding school in Lewisham and then won a scholarship to [[Eton College|Eton]]. He excelled at [[mathematics]] and won several prizes in the subject at the school, including the [[George Tomline (politician)#Tomline Prize|Tomline Prize]] in 1939 and the Russell Prize in 1940. He went on to [[Trinity College, Cambridge|Trinity College]], [[Cambridge]], where he again excelled, passing part one of the [[Mathematical Tripos|mathematical tripos]] as a [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]] in 1942 and part three in 1943 (the other three students to graduate from Cambridge after completing part three that year were [[Freeman Dyson]], [[James Lighthill]] and [[Fritz Ursell]], all of whom, like Skyrme, received [[British undergraduate degree classification#Variations in classification|starred first-class degrees]]<ref>{{cite news |title=UNIVERSITY AWARDS: CAMBRIDGE TRIPOS LISTS |work=The Times Educational Supplement |date=19 June 1943 |page=293}}</ref>). While there he was president of The [[Archimedeans]] mathematics society.<ref name="Dalitz">R. H. Dalitz, [http://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0217751X88001144?journalCode=ijmpa 'An outline of the life and work of Tony Skyrme'], International Journal of Modern Physics, A, 3 (1988), 2719–44 · The Times (3 July 1987) · CGPLA Eng. & Wales (1987)</ref>
<ref name="Peierls">Rudolf Peierls, ‘[http://odnb2.pubfactory.com/view/article/40677?docPos=&backToResults=%2Fsearch%2Fresults%2Fcontributors.jsp%3FcontributorId%3D551 Skyrme, Tony Hilton Royle (1922–1987)]{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}’, rev. Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Oxford University Press, 2004; online edn, Oct 2007</ref> 
<ref name="Champneys">''50 Visions of Mathematics'' Ed by Dara O Briain,   Chapter 10, page 38 by Alan Champneys, ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg8NBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA38 Tony Hilton Royle Skyrme]'', OUP Oxford, 2014, {{ISBN|9780191005336}}</ref>

With [[World War II|World War Two]] at its height after graduation he was drafted into war work as a mathematician under [[Rudolf Peierls]] who was leading a team working on the theoretical aspects of [[Atomic Energy for Military Purposes|atomic energy]], particularly as applied to [[Nuclear weapon|atomic weapons]].  At the end of 1943 Peierls and several other of the British scientists working on the  atom,  were transferred to the United States to assist in the [[Manhattan Project|Manhattan project]] to build a nuclear weapon. Skyrme followed  later in 1944, and worked on problems concerning the diffusion plant for isotope separation. He also used [[Punched card|IBM punch card tabulator]]s to calculate the implosions needed to detonate a [[Fat Man|plutonium bomb]]. His war time work earned him a [[Fellow|fellowship at Oxford]]. But he followed Peierls to the [[University of Birmingham]] where he became a [[research fellow]]. The [[academic year]]s 1948–49 and 1949–50 were spent at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton University|Princeton]], respectively. In 1949 he married Dorothy Mildred Millest, a lecturer in experimental nuclear physics whom he had met at Birmingham University. They had no children.<ref name="Dalitz"/><ref name="Peierls"/>

Returning to Britain both he and Dorothy gained posts at the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] at [[Harwell, Oxfordshire|Harwell]] from 1950 to 1962.  From 1954 he was head of the group there for theoretical nuclear physics, in which among others [[John Stewart Bell|
John Bell]] worked. Here he made two pioneering contributions to nuclear physics. One was to show how to handle short-range forces in a [[three-body problem]].  The other was a powerful approximation to nuclear forces, later widely used as the ‘[[Skyrme model]]’.<ref name="Peierls"/><ref name="Champneys"/>

In 1962 he proposed a mathematical  treatment of fundamental particles, in which particles such as [[neutron]]s and [[proton]]s, that  obey the [[Pauli exclusion principle]], appear as manifestations of fields such as that of [[meson]]s. These entities would later in 1982 become known as [[Skyrmion]]s. For this work Skyrme was awarded the [[Hughes Medal|Hughes medal]] of the [[Royal Society]] in 1985 but never received the full accolade of a [[Fellow of the Royal Society|fellowship]] there.<ref name="Champneys"/>

In 1958–59 he had travelled with his wife as tourists in a one-year overland circumnavigation of the globe by car and [[Land Rover Series|Land Rover]]. They fell in love with the lush tropical gardens of  [[Malaysia]] and decided to settle there.  In 1962 they left Harwell and Skyrme  took up a post in the [[University of Malaya]] in [[Kuala Lumpur]]. He found this involved heavy lecturing commitments and was less than stimulating to his research work and by 1964 had returned to Britain to a post as professor of [[Mathematical physics|Mathematical Physics]] at the  [[University of Birmingham]] where he remained for the rest of his career.<ref name="Peierls"/><ref name="Champneys"/>

His hobbies were [[home electronics]] – he built his own [[television]] receiver and [[High fidelity|Hi-Fi]] in the 1950s; and gardening, where he and Dorothy made an early attempt at [[self sufficiency]].<ref name="Champneys"/>

Tony was a keen amateur photographer and photographic collections from Tony and Dorothy's extensive travels are stored in the Bodleian Libraries Repository at the University of Oxford. Of particular interest in one collection are photos of a skiing trip in Saasfee, Switzerland in April 1947 with [[Rudolf Peierls]] and [[Klaus Fuchs]], some three years before Fuchs was convicted as a Soviet Spy.

Skyrme died on 25 June 1987 in Selly Oak Hospital, Birmingham, of an [[embolism]] after a routine  operation.<ref name="Peierls"/><ref name="Champneys"/>
